Part A — Examples of Conditional Statements

Example A: if ... else. Choose between two outcomes for a single value.
```{r}
score <- 78

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}
```
Example B: if ... else if ... else. Use it when there are more than two outcomes. R checks from top to bottom and stops at the first condition that is TRUE.
```{r}
score <- 86

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}
```
Example C: ifelse() for a whole vector. if works on one value at a time. ifelse() checks every element of a vector at once, which is what you need for a column of data.
```{r}
scores <- c(92, 68, 75, 81, 59)
ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
```
Example D: combining conditions. Use & when both conditions must be true and | when at least one must be true.
```{r}
grade <- 91
attendance <- 95

if (grade >= 90 & attendance >= 90) {
  print("Honors candidate")
}
```

Part B — Conditional Statements

Question #1 - Set temp <- 33. Print "Hot" if temp is 32 or higher, otherwise print "Not hot"
```{r}
temp <- 33
if (temp >= 32) {
  print("Hot")
} else {
  print("Not hot")
}
```
- The output is "Hot" because 33 is higher than 32.

Question #2 - Set age <- 17. Use if ... else if ... else to print "Child" for ages below 13, "Teenager" for 13 to 19, and "Adult" for 20 and above.

```{r}
age <- 17
if (age < 13) {
  print("Child")
} else if (age <= 19) {
  print("Teenager")
} else {
  print("Adult")
}
```
- The output is "Teenager" because 17 is between 13 and 19.

Question #3 - Create marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62). Use ifelse() to create a vector result that says "Pass" for marks of 60 or higher and "Fail" otherwise. Print result.

```{r}
marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
print(result)
```
- The output is "Fail" "Pass" "Pass" "Pass" "Pass".

Question #4 - Predict the output of the code below before you run it. Then run it and explain, in a comment, why you got that result.
```{r}
# Prediction: "A"
x <- 10
if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C")
}
# R goes through the conditions in order and runs only the first one that is TRUE, so every branch after it is ignored.
```

Question #5 - What is the difference between if and ifelse()? When would you choose each one?
- "if" makes one decision on a single value, while "ifelse()" gives a result for every element of a vector. Use "if" for one decision or a block of code, and "ifelse()" to fill a column of data.

Part C: Importing the CSV File

Question #6

a. Import the file safely.**
```{r}
file_path <- "students_grades.csv"
```

b. Use if ... else to check that the file exists before importing it.
```{r}
if (file.exists(file_path)) {
  grades <- read.csv(
    file_path,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
    na.strings = c("", "NA")
  )

} else {

}
```

```{r}

head(grades)

# Number of rows and columns
dim(grades)

# Column names
names(grades)

# Column data types
str(grades)

# Basic statistics
summary(grades)

```

d. Answer the following:
1. How many rows and columns does grades have?
- It has 15 rows and 7 columns

2. Which column contains missing values (NA), and how many?
- The Midterm column has one missing value.

3. What is the data type of the Section column?
- The Section column is character.

4. What are the lowest and highest Attendance values?
```{r}
range(grades$Attendance, na.rm = TRUE)
```

e. Check the grades should have 15 rows, 7 columns, and exactly one NA.
```{r}
if (
  nrow(grades) == 15 &&
  ncol(grades) == 7 &&
  sum(is.na(grades)) == 1
) {
  print("Check passed: 15 rows, 7 columns, and one missing value.")
} else {
  stop("The data does not match the expected structure.")
}
```

f. Applying Conditional Statements

f.1 Compute the final grade.** Any arithmetic with NA gives NA, so the student with the missing midterm will have NA as a final grade. This is expected.

```{r}
grades$FinalGrade <- (
  0.30 * grades$Quiz +
  0.30 * grades$Midterm +
  0.40 * grades$Final
)

grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade")]
```
- this computes the final grade; 30% for quiz, 30% for midterm and 40% for final and NA if missing midterm

f.2 Pass or fail.** Check for NA first, because NA >= 75 gives NA, not TRUE or FALSE.
```{r}
grades$Result <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Incomplete",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
)

grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Result")]
```
- 75 or higher pass and final grade with NA are marked as incomeplete

f.3 Grade remarks.** Replace each ___ with the correct cutoff or label, then change eval=FALSE to eval=TRUE in the chunk header.
```{r}
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Incomplete",
  ifelse(
    grades$FinalGrade >= 90,
    "Excellent",
    ifelse(
      grades$FinalGrade >= 85,
      "Very Good",
      ifelse(
        grades$FinalGrade >= 80,
        "Good",
        ifelse(
          grades$FinalGrade >= 75,
          "Fair",
          "Needs Improvement"
        )
      )
    )
  )
)

grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Remarks")]
```
- gives each student a remark

f.4 Attendance flag.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column AttendanceFlag with "At Risk" when Attendance is below 80 and "OK" otherwise.
```{r}
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(
  grades$Attendance < 80,
  "At Risk",
  "OK"
)

grades[, c("Name", "Attendance", "AttendanceFlag")]
```
-"At Risk" for students below 80 attendance

f.5 Honors candidates.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column Honors with "Yes" or "No". Use & to require both a final grade of 90 or higher and attendance of 90 or higher. Students with a missing final grade must get "No". Hint: use !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) as the first condition.

```{r}
grades$Honors <- ifelse(
  !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) &
    grades$FinalGrade >= 90 &
    grades$Attendance >= 90,
  "Yes",
  "No"
)

grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Attendance", "Honors")]
```
- Honors require a grade and attendance of atleast 90 and above.

f.6 if ... else if inside a loop.** ifelse() works on a whole column, but a plain if handles one value at a time. To use if on a column you must loop over the rows.
```{r}
for (i in seq_len(nrow(grades))) {
  if (is.na(grades$FinalGrade[i])) {
    grades$Result[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 75) {
    grades$Result[i] <- "Passed"
  } else {
    grades$Result[i] <- "Failed"
  }
}

grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Result")]
```

f.7 Now try if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") on its own in the Console. Explain the error or warning R gives and why the loop version avoids it.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed")
```
- R gives an error because "if" needs one condition,
but the column produces 15. The loop avoids this by checking one row at a time.

```{r}
}
```

Part D: Exporting Results to .csv
Question #7

a. Export the full processed table.** The argument row.names = FALSE stops R from adding an extra numbering column.
```{r}
write.csv(
  grades,
  "students_grades_processed.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```
b. Export the at-risk students.** The file is written only when there is at least one at-risk student.
```{r}
at_risk <- grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  write.csv(
    at_risk,
    "at_risk_students.csv",
    row.names = FALSE
  )

  print("At-risk students exported.")
} else {
  print("No at-risk students to export.")
}
```
c. Export the honors list.
```{r}
honors <- grades[
  grades$Honors == "Yes",
  c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")
]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(
    honors,
    "honors_list.csv",
    row.names = FALSE
  )

  print("Honors list exported.")
} else {
  print("No honors candidates to export.")
}
```
d. Verify your exports. Never assume a file was written correctly. Read it back and compare.
```{r}
processed_check <- read.csv(
  "students_grades_processed.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

print(all.equal(
  grades,
  processed_check,
  check.attributes = FALSE
))

if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  at_risk_check <- read.csv(
    "at_risk_students.csv",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  print(all.equal(
    at_risk,
    at_risk_check,
    check.attributes = FALSE
  ))
}

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  honors_check <- read.csv(
    "honors_list.csv",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  print(all.equal(
    honors,
    honors_check,
    check.attributes = FALSE
  ))
}
```
- each comparisons returned "TRUE"

Question #9

a. Add a column Scholarship to grades using these rules, then export the qualified students.
b. Use nested ifelse() statements. Test the missing grade first, then Full, then Partial

```{r}
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Pending",
  ifelse(
    grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
    "Full",
    ifelse(
      grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
      "Partial",
      "None"
    )
  )
)

grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Attendance", "Scholarship")]
```
- full scholarship requires grades 95 and above and attendance requires 90 and above for partial 85 above for grade and 90 above for attendance "NA" gets pending

c. Select students whose Scholarship is "Full" or "Partial". Hint: %in% c("Full", "Partial").
```{r}
scholarship_candidates <- grades[
  grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"),
]

scholarship_candidates
```

d. Export them to scholarship_candidates.csv with row.names = FALSE, using an if ... else guard
```{r}
if (nrow(scholarship_candidates) > 0) {
  write.csv(
    scholarship_candidates,
    "scholarship_candidates.csv",
    row.names = FALSE
  )

  print("Scholarship candidates exported.")
} else {
  print("No qualified scholarship candidates.")
}
```

e. Print a count of each category with table().
```{r}
table(grades$Scholarship)
```
- There are 1 Full, 9 None, 4 Partial, and 1 Pending 

Question #10
```{r}
#1. Why did you check is.na() before comparing the final grade to a number?
## Comparing anything to NA gives NA, so deal with missing grades before running the comparison

#2. In Task 3.2, what would happen if the Failed condition were placed before the Incomplete condition?
## If "Failed" is checked first, FinalGrade < 75 returns NA for a missing grade. A plain if would stop with an error, while ifelse() would quietly give that student NA.

#3. When is ifelse() the better choice than if ... else, and when is if ... else better?
## Use ifelse() when you're working on a whole vector, such as a column of grades. Use if ... else for a single decision, such as whether or not to export a file.

#4. Why is it useful to read an exported CSV back into R?
## Reading an exported CSV back into R lets you confirm that it saved properly and that the values are unchanged.
```
